binders: A nonnegative real rate parameter lambda.
conclusions: The real-valued Poisson(lambda) measure of {n in the natural numbers : t <= n} is at most exp(-lambda) * ((e * lambda) / t)^t, where the power is real exponentiation.
mathematical_definitions: The left side is the real conversion of the Poisson measure of the natural-number upper-tail set.
The exponentiation ((e * lambda) / t)^t is Real.rpow with real base and real exponent.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every nonnegative rate lambda and every real t strictly larger than lambda, a Poisson random count with rate lambda has upper-tail probability at most exp(-lambda) times ((e lambda)/t) raised to the real power t: P(N >= t) <= exp(-lambda) ((e lambda)/t)^t. The event is expressed directly as the set of natural numbers n satisfying t <= n.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The rate is restricted to nonnegative real values.
The threshold must satisfy t > lambda; since lambda >= 0, this also guarantees t > 0 and makes division by t nonzero.
The statement covers only the strict upper-threshold regime and says nothing for t <= lambda, including t = lambda.
Because samples are natural numbers but t is real, the event t <= n is effectively an integer upper tail with the threshold rounded up, although no ceiling operation appears explicitly.
The power is real exponentiation (Real.rpow), so its edge-value conventions matter; the hypotheses make its base nonnegative, and at lambda = 0 the base is zero with positive exponent.
The proposition is stated directly for a measure on natural numbers, not for an arbitrary random variable merely assumed to have that distribution.
The premise is satisfiable for every nonnegative lambda by choosing any t > lambda; there is no apparent vacuity from the main hypothesis.
ambiguities: The dossier stops at the external frontier defining the measure via poissonPMF and does not expand the point-mass formula or normalization of that PMF.
The dossier identifies real power as Real.rpow but does not expand its definition, so special-case conventions such as a zero base are inherited from that library operation.
